name: Risk parity (inverse volatility asset allocation)

origin.source_title: Leverage Aversion and Risk Parity (Financial Analysts Journal)

how_it_works.simple: Give each type of investment the same amount of wobble instead of the same amount of money. Calm things get more money, jumpy things get less.
how_it_works.analogy: Like loading a canoe so every paddler carries the same effort, rather than giving each the same size bag.
how_it_works.precise: Weights are set proportional to the inverse of each asset class's estimated volatility, so each contributes similar risk; the whole portfolio is then scaled (often with borrowing) to a target volatility. Asness, Frazzini and Pedersen argue that leverage-averse investors overprice risky assets, so safer assets like bonds carry higher risk-adjusted returns that a levered risk parity portfolio can collect.

rule: At each month end, set the weight of each asset class to k divided by its volatility, estimated from the past 36 monthly excess returns; choose k so the portfolio hits a volatility target (for example the volatility of a 60/40 or market portfolio); rebalance monthly.
data_needed: Monthly total returns for equities, government bonds, credit, commodities
economic_rationale: Leverage aversion makes low-risk assets offer higher Sharpe ratios; risk parity overweights them and applies leverage (Asness, Frazzini and Pedersen 2012; Frazzini and Pedersen 2014).
why_it_might_fail: It depends on bonds staying a good diversifier and on cheap borrowing; in 2022 stocks and bonds fell together (S&P 500 -18.0%, 10-year Treasury -17.8% per Damodaran), the setting where a bond-heavy levered portfolio is hurt most.

reported_results.notes: Annual excess return over T-bills. Leverage chosen to match the ex post volatility of the value-weighted benchmark, which uses hindsight for scaling only. Trading costs not explicitly deducted; financing discussed in the paper's Appendix B.

reported_results.notes: Annual excess return over T-bills; value-weighted benchmark in the same sample had a Sharpe ratio of 0.43.

post_publication_evidence: The 2012 paper's sample ends in 2010, during a long bond rally. The catalog did not find a verifiable post-2012 risk parity index series to quote; the 2022 joint stock and bond loss (Damodaran data) is the main known stress for the approach.

implementations.notes: Portfolio optimization library with risk parity and risk budgeting models.

relevance.reason: The same inverse-volatility weighting can size FX positions, and it is a common multi-asset benchmark.
